_on_ [June 6, 2025](https://downthetubes.net/in-review-doctor-who-wish-world-the-reality-war/ "12:29 pm")

_In “**Wish World**”, traps are sprung and old enemies unite as the Doctor and Belinda finally arrive home to find a very different world. Can the Doctor see the truth before midnight arrives? The story concludes in “**The Reality War**”… Battle rages across the skies as the Unholy Trinity unleash their deadly ambition. The Doctor, Belinda and Ruby have to risk everything in the quest to save one innocent life…_

**SPOILERS AHEAD**

**_Review by Tim Robins_**

![Image 1: Doctor Who - Wish World - Illustration by Fraser Geesin](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Fraser-Geesin-DW-Wish-World-1024x1024.jpeg)

![Image 2: Doctor Who - Reality War - Illustration by Fraser Geesin](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Fraser-Geesin-DW-Reality-War-1024x1024.jpeg)

_Illustrations by Fraser Geesin_

The two-part finale to the latest _Doctor Who_ season started well, but concluded in a series of talky reshoots, aimed at beefing up Ncuti Gatwa’s departure in role of The Doctor. There was lots to look at, and Gatwa & Co were in good form but, in the end, it was all a bit glum.

The end of _Doctor Who_, Season Two (2025) has already attracted a lot of online controversy and recrimination, as news that the  show is no longer in production gathers traction. I must admit, a lot of what kept me watching “The Reality War” was waiting to hear the fate of the programme because, autistically, I felt the BBC had promised to announce this after Season Two had been transmitted. Obviously, I now realise that they didn’t mean _immediately_ after. What we got instead was a trailer for “The War Between The Land and the Sea” and newspaper coverage of Gatwa’s regeneration, or rather who he regenerated into.

I must admit, word of the halt in production has cast a shadow over my enthusiasm for the new _Doctor Who_ episodes. Eagle-eyed readers may notice that I asked the illustrator Fraser Geesin to spell out ‘axed’ on The Doctor’s fingers for my review of “**[Lux](https://downthetubes.net/in-review-doctor-who-lux/)**”. I doubt that the BBC is going to announce the end of _Doctor Who_ production, although a simple “_Doctor Who_ will return” would at least give fans hope.

If you are looking for anger, you’ve come to the wrong review. I’m not interested in accusatory finger-pointing at showrunner Russell T. Davies’ return to the show. Nor will blame Ncuti Gatwa’s portrayal of The Doctor. I am not shilling for the BBC or Disney+, I’m just going to give my penny’s worth on the final episodes.

Also, poring over this or that continuity point is best left to those fans who are concerned about such things. That can be fun, but I’m just not in that place anymore. If pressed on the regeneration, I’d note that The Doctor, notably as played by Colin Baker and Peter Capaldi, has taken on the appearance of characters who have appeared in the show and has even revisited past regenerations, i.e. Tom Baker as The Curator.

I was surprised with the news brought to us by The Rani, that Time Lords are sterile. That’s because The Doctor has a grand-daughter and parents. So, thanks to award-winning author Peter Anghelides for drawing my attention back to the script, which explained that this was a recent event, and that bi-generation was nature’s work-around to continue the Time Lord race. This is just one of the strands that may or may not be continued in Big Finish audio adventures or other fan fiction.

![Image 3](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/IMG_3581-1024x577.jpg)

_Doctor Who – Wish World. The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) | James Pardon/BBC Studios/Disney/Bad Wolf_

“Wish World” certainly engaged my interest. The episode opened with the familiar trope of our hero living an apparently utopian life in the London suburbs – in reality, a dystopian place at the best of times. The Rani, wonderfully played by Archie Panjabi as a swaggering dominatrix, has harnessed the Pantheon’s wish god and yoked this to the limited imagination of Conrad Clark (previously seen in “**[Lucky Day](https://downthetubes.net/in-review-doctor-who-lucky-day/)**”, earlier on the season).

We learn in “The Reality War” that The Rani’s aim is to rerun the same day over and over again, in order to wear away reality, and open it up to an extradimensional underworld where dwells Omega, the Time Lord who invented time travel, went mad, and now wants to become nothing less than the God of Time. _Yikes!_ If you think that’s a massive task for The Rani, it certainly was for the effects team. London falling through reality to the depths of the Underworld, was envisaged unreadably as a swarm of purple pixels.

In “Wish World”, we were immersed in The Rani’s reality bubble – a weird place in which The Doctor and Mel are neighbours and gigantic bone creatures stalk the streets, oblivious to the lives below. Worse, the population is glued to a _Jackanory_\-style TV show in which Conrad reads the Doctor’s adventures to viewers.

Amusingly, Conrad’s collection of _Doctor Who_ stories had self-referential titles that echoed the way Target adaptations would rename stories for example, retitling “The Silurians” as _Doctor Who and the Cave Monsters_. In this case, the titles included _Doctor Who and the Deadly Wish_, _Doctor Who and the Big Bad Wolf_ and _Doctor Who and the English Rose_. It was all so “meta”!

![Image 4](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/IMG_3590-1024x682.jpg)

_Doctor Who – Wish World. Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King) | James Pardon/BBC Studios/Disney/Bad Wolf_

In the alternate reality, The Doctor and Belinda were married, and The Doctor and his companion in bed together was as startling as it was intended to be. On top of that, they have a child! And, yes, it’s Captain Poppy, a welcome return of the adorable child actress, Sienna-Robyn Mavanga Phillips. How and why Captain Poppy came from the future to be in Conrad’s pocket universe and, earlier, make a guest appearance in “**[The Story and The Engine](https://downthetubes.net/in-review-doctor-who-the-story-the-engine/)**” is anyone’s guess. But there’s no surprise as to why the talented young actress got to reprise her role. Although, thanks to reshoots, she then went on to be central to The Doctor’s need to regenerate.

This being _Doctor Who_, “Wish World” had some smart social commentary, such as when Ruby (Millie Gibson), also part of this new reality,  encounters UNIT’s scientific advisor, Shirley Bingham (Ruth Madeley), a wheelchair user who now lives in a makeshift camp with other disabled citizens, displaced because people with disabilities are beyond Conrad’s limited imagination. A timely reminder that you can write people out of reality, but they still exist.

The other downside of the reality bubble is that people are expected to inform on anyone doubting its reality. This led to Orwellian scenes of friends, family and loved ones informing on each other and security guards turning up to cart everyone away in the backs of vans. This has a new, chilling resonance since America has started “disappearing people” from its streets. From the comparative safety of Britain, I can only imagine the fear and justifiable paranoia this must create, and only hope it doesn’t happen here.

Events come together at the towering Bone Palace, a new addition to London’s skyline and “Wish World” ends with reality finally collapsing under its own weight, Omega announcing his return and an over-the-cliff-edge moment as a balcony breaks away from the Tower and The Doctor falls to certain death…

… Until he is rescued by Anita Benn (Steph de Whalley), a receptionist of The Time Hotel in the preceding Christmas Special, the woeful Steven Moffat penned “**[Joy to the World](https://downthetubes.net/in-review-doctor-who-joy-to-the-world-christmas-special/)**”. Benn has been opening the hotel’s time doors to find The Doctor, who she has a crush on. “The Reality War” had an amusing, running gag as Anita became caught up in more and more cosmic goings-on and had to remind people that she was only a member of staff in a hotel! Clearly, the hospitality industry has become a lot more challenging over time.

![Image 5](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/DW02-02-08-Anita-and-Doctor-1024x682.jpg)

_Anita (Steph De Whalley) The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) | Photo: Lara Cornell/BBC Studios/Bad Wolf_

According to Davies, the Time Hotel was suggested by Steven Moffat as a way out for The Doctor should he ever fall from a balcony at some point – a scenario proposed by Davies. It should be noted that as far as _Doctor Who_ goes, the concept of the Time Hotel, which allows guests to enjoy temporal vacations, was first introduced in a comic strip, “**[Hotel Historia](https://tardis.wiki/wiki/Hotel_Historia_/(comic_story/))**”, written by **Dan McDaid** for _Doctor Who Magazine_, first published in 2008 and collected in **_The Crimson Hand_**, which includes an introduction by Russell T. Davies.

![Image 6](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/DW02-02-08-Conrad-Rani-1024x682.jpg)

_Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King) Rani (Archie Panjabi) | Photo: James Pardon/BBC Studios/Bad Wolf_

Things gather pace as Ruby gets to chat with Conrad. We learn that he became a fascist due to poor parenting (!?), to continue the show’s abysmal explanation for mysogynistic online trolling. At this point, Davies threw caution to the wind. Omega, or perhaps ‘The Beast of Omega’ (as an eagle-eyed fan noted was how the creature was referred to in the BBC’s subtitles) pops up out of the underverse, only to swallow Archie Panjabi’s Rani whole. (The Rani’s fate got a laugh from me. Sudden juxtapositions lend themselves to comedy. Mrs Flood snuck off to bi-generate again, one presumes).

I was also pleasantly surprised by an unexpected guest appearance by the Thirteenth Doctor. It is said that Gatwa himself did not know Jodie Whittaker would be returning to her role. Their exchange was poignant and a great call back to the unfairly-maligned Chibnall era. Jodie’s energetic reappearance must surely have been engineered by Davies to provide maximum fury and discomfort for “fans” who spent five years screaming “#notmydoctor” into cyberspace.

![Image 7](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/DW02-02-08-2-Doctors-L-1024x682.jpg)

_The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) The Doctor (Jodie Whittaker) | Photo: James Pardon/BBC Studios/Bad Wolf_

Davies loves _Doctor Who_. He seems to effortlessly recall the show’s past and reimagine old characters as new. He also gleefully plays with fans’ expectations. This playfulness can be confusing. I still don’t understand the character of Susan Triad (Susan Twist) who, together with the actress’s name, remained nothing more than a red herring. The only “twist” was that she had nothing to do with Susan (the Doctor’s granddaughter) nor the ‘Triad’ i.e. the Unholy Trinity of Conrad, Mrs Rani Flood or The Rani – the definitive article as it were.

I honestly thought that the past appearances of Susan (Carol Anne Ford, looking nothing like her 80-plus years) was setting up Season Three, so I was not at all surprised that her thread was not tied up in this episode. For continuity buffs, Belinda keeps Poppy safe from changes in reality by entering a “Zero Room”. This safety device was last seen in Peter Davison’s “**[Castrovalva](https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p00v7crf)**”, back in 1982. The mention here did seem a bit throw-away, although Castrovalva also featured an invented reality, albeit one shaped from the mathematical mind of Adric.

![Image 8](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/DW02-02-08-Omega-L-1024x507.jpg)

_Omega | Photo: BBC Studios/Bad Wolf_

In many ways, “Wish World/The Reality War” was a wish list for fans, with the proviso that you need to be careful what you wish for. Fans have long requested the return of The Rani, and this story gave us two for the price of one. There has also been a hankering for old foes. So we had Sutekh at the end of Season One, then Omega at the end of this season.

It is, therefore, really churlish to find the very same fans pulling the rug from under this by claiming such continuity references aren’t meaningful to the general public. To which I say, make your flipping minds up  – do you want old enemies or not? Also, you’ve discovered the internet. iPlayer’s Whoniverse is a bridge to the past. And what’s a bridge for? _[Crossing!](https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episodes/p0gglvqn/doctor-who)_ OK… the CGI Omega beast was a bit shonky on the effects front, but that’s totally in line with the climaxes of much of Disney’s superhero output.

![Image 9: In the end, while cast were on good form, the two-part finale was all a bit glum](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/DW02-02-08-Regeneration-2-1024x556.jpg)

_The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) | Photo: James Pardon/BBC Studios/Bad Wolf_

I am sorry to see Gatwa go. The BBC’s silence on his departure has led to speculation that he was sacked or, as one commentator had it “asked to leave”. I really don’t think he was. There has been ludicrous speculation that Gatwa was dismissed because he pulled out of a guest appearance at _The Eurovision Song Contest_. This has to be malicious gossip, or plain ignorance of _Doctor Who_’s production. Seasons One and Two were filmed almost back-to-back. I understand that Gatwa’s regeneration, although added later, was recorded while Season One was being transmitted. And _The Eurovision Song Contest_ is transmitted _live_, for goodness sake.

Gatwa is, at time of writing, one of only two other Doctors who I wish had stayed for more seasons. One was Jon Pertwee, the other was Matt Smith. I think Gatwa brought tremendous energy to the role and, despite the bi-generation schtick, decisively stepped out of David Tennant’s shadow.

It’s sad that some people are hiding behind the word “woke”. What they really mean, but don’t say, is that they don’t like having to watch a gay black man in the role of The Doctor. There’s a whole lack of acceptance of human rights, right now – foremost of which is the right to exist and be included and to be heard.

What I want to see is more _Doctor Who_, but, for the moment, production of new episodes has been stopped. I’m not going to quibble over whether this is a “hiatus hernia”, “bed rest” or cancellation. Production has stopped. A key difference between the 1980s and now is that, back then, there wasn’t much enthusiasm within the BBC for _Doctor Who_’s immediate return. The BBC do want the programme back on air but, I understand, they are aware of _Doctor Who’_s sharp decline since Moffat cast Peter Capaldi, and thereby lost the show’s young audience.

I think that the BBC see themselves as acting in _Doctor Who_’s interest, notably to protect the ‘brand’. The only questions that remain are _when_ will _Doctor Who_return, and how will it be paid for. The answers are unknown to me at this time.

I will say that Bad Wolf and Davies gave it their best shot. It missed its mark, but no one can say that they didn’t bring something new, creative and bold to the table, even if it did fall through the cracks in reality and end up looking rather broken by the fall.

But fear not, true believers! One day _Doctor Who_ will come back. Yes it will come back. Until then, there must be no regrets, no anxieties, just fact check all your beliefs, because I know I am not mistaken in mine.

Ooh, I almost forgot, drum roll, stop the presses, the new Doctor is **Billie Piper**! Ta da! LMAO. Well, maybe. I saw her appearance simply as RTD calling in a favour and having a bit of fun. It certainly caught the press’s attention, and I see Big Finish are already promoting their adventures of Rose and at a 25 per cent discount.

For now, I’m off, but I’ll be back, certainly before production on a new series of _Doctor Who_ begins again.

**_Tim Robins_**

Whew! Well, that was a rollercoaster of a ride.

There are numerous backstories and historical references that we’ll likely need a special article or two to unpack. So, we’ll skip most of these nostalgia Easter eggs—nods to fans like me and my Blogtor colleagues—and focus on the review proper. However, for clarity, we can’t avoid a brief historical lesson on Doctor Who lore.

### **Time Lord Scientists**

The Rani, originally played by Kate O’Mara, appeared in _“The Mark of the Rani”_ (1985) and _“Time and the Rani”_ (1987). She was a renegade Time Lord scientist, amoral rather than evil, who conducted experiments on other species for her own research. Unlike the Master’s obsession with the Doctor, the Rani was dismissive of such petty rivalries, considering herself above such childish games. Although not seen on screen, the extended universe suggests that she, the Doctor, and the Master were fellow students at the Time Lord Academy on Gallifrey.

Omega, meanwhile, is even more steeped in Time Lord mythology. First appearing in the 10th anniversary story _“The Three Doctors”_ (1972-73), he was one of the founding fathers of Time Lord civilisation—a stellar engineer who created the supernova that became the Eye of Harmony, enabling time travel. Trapped in an antimatter universe for aeons by Rassilon, he has appeared sporadically since, most notably in _“Arc of Infinity”_ (1983) and briefly in _“The Timeless Children”_ (2020). He is known for sustaining himself in exile through sheer willpower and imagination.

The Rani is back! And Omega seems to be returning for the finale. Cue the return of the Time Lord scientists.

### **The First Half of the Story**

_“Wish World”_ is essentially half an episode, with the second half scheduled to air next week. It’s a setup for the grand finale, and whilst that makes for compelling television, it leaves _“Wish World”_ somewhat incomplete as a standalone story.

Russell T Davies continues his fairytale-and-gods thread with the introduction of the Wish Baby—the seventh son of seventh son of the seventh son—who can make his wishes reality. By exploiting both the Wish Baby and Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King) from _“Lucky Day,”_ Earth, the Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa), Belinda (Varada Sethu), and their friends are trapped in a dystopian version of Earth.

[![Image 1: Doctor Who - S2E7 - Wish World 0 Conrad (JONAH HAUER-KING) BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520867.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520867-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

Doctor Who – S2E7 – Wish World 0 Conrad (JONAH HAUER-KING) BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon

Director Alex Pillai highlights the contrast between the bright, artificial perfection of the wish world and the menace lurking beneath. We’re thrust into an alternate reality where the Doctor is John Smith, happily married to Belinda with their daughter Poppy,  last seen in “Space Babies”, living in a pastel-coloured dystopia that would make The Stepford Wives blush. Pillai particularly shines in domestic scenes, where perfection cracks—quite literally—as the Doctor’s mugs shatter every time he experiences doubt.  Davies effectively leverages doubt as the power capable of destroying Earth on May Day. The idea that a Time Lord’s doubt could crack open the universe is brilliantly apocalyptic in scope.

[![Image 2: The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) and Poppy (SIENNA-ROBYN MAVANGA-PHIPPS), in Wish World COPYRIGHT:BBC Studios,CREDIT LINE:BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/Dan Fearon. The Doctor, in a r-piece suit with the jacket removed, sits in front of Poppy in her high chair in a regular suburban kitchen, looking at her lovingly](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520879.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520879-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) and Poppy (SIENNA-ROBYN MAVANGA-PHIPPS), in Wish World COPYRIGHT:BBC Studios,CREDIT LINE:BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/Dan Fearon

### **Social Commentary with a Side of Nostalgia**

Davies isn’t subtle about his critique of conservative values. There’s a pointed dig at Harry Potter through Conrad’s storybook styling. His utopia—where women stay at home, men wear bowler hats, and those deemed “different” are rendered invisible—feels alarmingly plausible, even more so in 2025 than when this episode was written and filmed.  The paranoia and thought policing evoke real-world echoes, making the dystopia chilling rather than camp.

The costume department deserves praise. While cosplay analysis is the domain of fellow Blogtor writer Peter, I must commend the designers for the full-leather creation paying tribute to the Rani’s classic red design. Much appreciated by this classic Who fan.

### **Character Carousel**

We see the return of Mel (Bonnie Langford), Shirley (Ruth Madeley), Ruby (Millie Gibson), baby Poppy, Rogue (Jonathan Groff), Kate Stewart (Jemma Redgrave), and Colonel Ibrahim (Alexander Devrient). It’s clear preparation for the UNIT spin-off, _The War Between the Land and the Sea_. Doctor Who, like many long-running shows, tends to pack finales with returning characters. While it’s a crowd-pleasing approach, it can come at the cost of depth. We must wait and see how the finale handles the large cast.

Ruby’s mother and grandmother turning her in again raises uncomfortable questions about familial loyalty. Are they really the best support for our former companion? Meanwhile, Groff’s return as Rogue delivers one of the more emotional moments, albeit a fleeting one.

[![Image 3: Doctor Who Wish World - The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) Melanie Bush (BONNIE LANGFORD), BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520875.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/520875-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

Doctor Who Wish World – The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) Melanie Bush (BONNIE LANGFORD), BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon

### **The Rani Conundrum**

Archie Panjabi clearly relishes playing the Rani, bringing theatrical menace reminiscent of Kate O’Mara, while making the role her own. However, her motivation is puzzling. The original Rani was fascinating because she wasn’t interested in domination—she was a pure scientist with no moral compass. She famously dismissed the Doctor and the Master’s rivalry as childish.

This version seems to be more traditionally villainous, which, while entertaining, diverges from the character’s original uniqueness.  The Rani was never a follower; she was independent and dismissive of other Time Lords’ schemes. Her classic-era experiments—like turning people into trees—were clinical, not malicious. Why she would want to enable Omega’s return remains unclear, especially as he might regard her and her experiments as trivial.

The dynamic between Mrs Flood (Anita Dobson) and the “new” Rani is compelling. Dobson remains unnerving, and there are signs of tension that suggest Mrs Flood might represent the traditional Rani, while Panjabi’s version may have been corrupted by time spent in the underverse.

[![Image 4: The Rani (Archie Panjabi) Mrs Flood/aka The Rani (Anita Dobson) - BBC Studios/Bad Wolf](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/JPP-WHO-170524-7.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/JPP-WHO-170524-7-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

The Rani (Archie Panjabi) Mrs Flood /Aka The Rani (Anita Dobson) – BBC Studios / Bad Wolf

### **Questions, Questions Everywhere**

“Wish World” leaves a staggering number of unanswered questions: What’s Poppy’s true significance? Where is Belinda when she vanishes? What role does Omega play?

The Omega reveal is particularly intriguing from a lore standpoint. In “The Three Doctors,” he was driven mad by isolation, sustained only by imagination, not unlike Conrad’s wish-world. If the Rani is trying to use him, she may be playing with forces beyond even her intellect.

[![Image 5: Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King) The Rani (Archie Panjabi) Mrs Flood/aka The Rani (Anita Dobson): Wish World's Unholy Trinity BBC Studios/Bad Wolf. Contrad, in futuristic white suit, the Rani in blood red leather biker jacket and skirt, and Mrs. Flood, in black touser suit, look down at the viewer from a dias in a room that looks like it's constructed of bone](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/090524-JPP-WHO-00630.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/090524-JPP-WHO-00630-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King) The Rani (Archie Panjabi) Mrs Flood/aka The Rani (Anita Dobson): Wish World’s Unholy Trinity BBC Studios/Bad Wolf

### Final Thoughts

“Wish World” works as spectacle and setup, even if it feels incomplete on its own. Davies has always excelled at emotional beats, and this episode sets up what could be a powerful finale.

The episode shines in its critique of Conrad’s “perfect” world and its timely social commentary. It’s less successful when mired in Time Lord mythology and exposition. Despite the visual flair and character cameos, the heart of the story—the terrifying Wish Baby and its implications—gets a bit lost.

Still, as a penultimate episode, _“Wish World”_ does its job. It raises the stakes, brings back beloved characters, and sets up a potentially epic conclusion. Whether it all pays off remains to be seen, but there’s no denying Davies has created something bold and visually stunning.

Now, about those bone dinosaurs…

[![Image 6: The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) in Wish World ,BBC Studios,Dan Fearon/ The Doctor, in smart business suit, leans forward, his arms resting on the table in front of him, hands folded, as he stares seriously directly into the camera](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/517536.jpg?resize=696%2C464&quality=89)](https://i0.wp.com/www.blogtorwho.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/517536-scaled.jpg?quality=89)

The Doctor (NCUTI GATWA) in Wish World ,BBC Studios,Dan Fearon

**Doctor Who** concludes with _The Reality War_ at 6.50pm GMT next Saturday on **BBC One** in the UK and Ireland, and on Disney+ everywhere else. It will also be in cinemas in a double bill with Wish World starting at 6pm in most locations ([find your local screening here](https://www.doctorwhoincinemas.co.uk/home/))

Shirley: Yeah, but you're different from us lot. Pardon me if I don't frisk you, but you seem very non-disabled to me.  
Ruby: Oh! Ha! Well, I could be taller. But, yeah.

Synopsis
--------

Bavaria, 1865: In a shack in a forest Otto welcomes the Rani, who he assumes is the midwife, to help with the delivery of his and Violett's child. The child has already been born by the time she arrives. Luckily all is well, although as the seventh son of a seventh son Otto has always been lucky. Otto also now has seven sons of his own. With a breath the Rani transforms Violett into Violets, Otto into an owl, and Otto's first six suns into ducks before leaving with the newborn - Jonas.

London, 23rd May 2025 07:00: Mr John Smith and Belinda awake to another day, and are soon interrupted by their child, Poppy. Belinda turns on the TV where Conrad Clark promises that the weather will be nice - across the UK, Great Britain, and the world.

Conrad appears continuously on TV all around the world. He starts the day with a story - Doctor Who and the Deadly Wish. Downstairs Mr Smith isn't really paying attention as he gives Poppy her breakfast whilst Belinda is preparing for cleaning and shopping. Belinda asks Poppy if she is looking forward to the day, and when Poppy says no a cup drops through the table smashes on the floor. Belinda cleans up the broken cup as Mr Smith heads to work.

As Mr Smith leaves for work he finds a woman on his doorstep, Ruby, who asks if he is known as the Doctor. When Ruby sees Poppy she tells Mr Smith that he doesn't have a daughter. AS Belinda becomes hostile, and makes a telephone call about Ruby expressing doubt, Ruby leaves. In the street she meets sees neighbours people taking out broken cups, including Melanie.

Ruby follows the Doctor, unseen, to where he works, and watches as he passes by a woman in a wheelchair - Shirley. Inside UNIT - the Unified National Insurance Team - the Doctor makes it to his desk with minutes to spare as the tea-lady, Susan, offers Mr Smith a cup of tea. Mr Smith starts talking to a c-worker, Christofer, who fancies their boss, Kate. Christofer is nervous about approaching Kate, and Mr Smith says he is a beautiful man and has nothing to worry about. Christofer's attitude changes at the idea of a man finding another man beautiful as Mr Smith's cup of tea falls through his desk.

As Mr Smith begins work at home Belinda welcomes her mum and auntie Devika. Poppy is being cheeky, but Devika says there is time to drum that out of her so she grows up to be a good little girl, good little wife, then good little mother, like all women should be - according to Conrad, who is never wrong. The conversation turns to the birth of Poppy, and as Belinda struggles to remember another cup crashes through the table.

The Rani has a palace overlooking London where she, Mrs Flood, and Conrad Clark, are based. Conrad is in his room and pauses his transmission as Mrs Flood serves him a sandwich. Conrad is exhausted with all the thinking, and Mrs Flood reassures him that he's doing a very good job as the boy who wants the world to be better. In the corner of the room is a baby - Jonas - who is sustaining the whole world.

Outside UNIT Ruby and Shirley start to recognise each other and Shirley leads Ruby to an encampment where the disabled, and the dispossessed, the ones who do not fit in, live. Ruby tells Shirley she has doubts about the world as she had lived through a different version of 2025. (See [73 Yards](https://www.mentalis.co.uk/ncuti-gatwa/73-yards)). Shirley explains that even though the people in the camp have nothing they are somehow okay. Shirley has no money but has a state of the art wheelchair. And somehow everything is connected to Conrad Clark.

Brian, who is blind, has a theory that as Conrad is not disabled he literally cannot see them. And as Conrad has somehow become God of the Earth, Shirley says they have a plan to take down God. A fully charged tablet, a relic from the Old World, shows the location of Conrad, and may offer a way to block his transmission.

At home Mr Smith, alone with his thoughts, sees things in the TV - including a seeing his granddaughter, Susan, and Rogue, trapped in a hell dimension who gives Doctor a strange warning: Tables don't do that. Upstairs Belinda is awoken by the sounds of cups smashing. In the kitchen she sees Mr Smith and loads of smashed cups. He places on on the table and a few moments later it slips though the table.

To Belinda these slips are normal. As Mr Smith is starting to doubt she makes a telephone call. Shortly afterwards police arrive and take the Doctor away. One of the police is Mrs Flood, and Belinda is taken away as well. Mr Smith and Belinda are taken to the Rani's bone palace.

Inside the palace the Rani tries to jog Mr Smith's memory about who he really is. As the time gets closer to 24th May 2025,n the Rani tells Mr Smith who she is, and the Doctor starts to remember. The Rani tells Belinda that the whole world is just a wish, and that the Doctor had stirred the gods and woke the most ancient of powers. The Rani shows the Doctor the room where Conrad is holding the baby who is the god of wishes - Desiderium.

The Rani boosted the baby's power using the Vindicator to create a web of titanic Voystet-Bladen energy that allowed Conrad to create an entire world. But the world is unable to sustain itself which leads to doubts. The Rani explains she needed the Doctor trapped inside the wish. Normal doubts cracks the structure of reality, but a Time Lords's doubt would rip it open.

The Rani leads the Doctor to a balcony. He can see London and the huge wholes opening up. The Rani wants to destroy the wished world so she can see the Underverse hidden underneath where the One Who Is Lost is hidden - Omega, the creator of the Time Lords.

As the Doctor finally remembers who he is he finds himself alone on the balcony. Back inside the palace the Rani triggers explosives and the balcony plummets towards London.

Doctor Who Season Two is launching worldwide on April 12th. “The Robot Revolution” will debut exclusively on BBC iPlayer at 8am and later in the day on BBC One in the UK. Viewers outside the UK can watch Doctor Who simultaneously on Disney+.

Following the premiere, new episodes will be released weekly.  The 15th Doctor, Ncuti Gatwa and his companions, Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu) and Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson) will be accompanied by an impressive roster of guest stars including Emmy Award winner Alan Cumming as cartoon villain Mr Ring-a-Ding, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Anita Dobson, Bonnie Langford, Jemma Redgrave, Ruth Madeley, Susan Twist, Caoilfhionn Dunne, Christopher Chung, Evelyn Miller, Ariyon Bakare, Julie Dray, Michelle Greenidge, Angela Wynter, Alexander Devrient, Rylan, Freddie Fox, Jonah Hauer-King, and Kadiff Kirwan, among many others.  Just in case, you didn’t catch it from the list of guest stars, Mrs Flood and Unit are definitely back.

 

The episode titles, writers and directors are all announced.

Doctor Who – Season Two | Episode Titles:
-----------------------------------------

1.  **The Robot Revolution** – Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Peter Hoar
2.  **Lux** – Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Amanda Brotchie
3.  **The Well** – Written by Russell T Davies & Sharma Angel Walfall, directed by Amanda Brotchie
4.  **Lucky Day** – Written by Pete McTighe, directed by Peter Hoar
5.  **The Story & the Engine** – Written by Inua Ellams, directed by Makalla McPherson
6.  **The Interstellar Song Contest** – Written by Juno Dawson, directed by Ben A. Williams
7.  **Wish World** – Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai

##### [‘Dog Love Stories’ is a Heartfelt Book by Patricia Eagle](https://outfrontmagazine.com/dog-love-stories-is-a-heartfelt-book-by-patricia-eagle/ "TV Review: ‘Doctor Who’ Episode “Wish World” Presents Us With a Horrifying Heteronormative Dystopia")

![Image 9](https://outfrontmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/OFM_trust.jpg)

The right wing has made it very clear that their ultimate goal is to return us to a version of the 1950s that never really existed, where gender roles are never challenged and LGBTQ+ people don’t exist, a world where men go to work and women stay home with babies and nobody ever questions the way of things. This week’s _Doctor Who_ gives us a terrifying glimpse into a world just like that, a version of 2025 wished into being by an incel. It’s a terrifying dystopian nightmare, but it’s clearly the kind that conservatives on both sides of the Atlantic are trying to build, and the episode reminds us how important it is to resist such a world from ever being built.

**But that’s as much as I’m willing to tell you before I give you my spoiler warning for this week, so don’t read on if you don’t want to be spoiled for “Wish World.”**

![Image 10](https://outfrontmagazineimages.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/26124554/sa900793_eefddab1.jpeg)The episode starts with one of the newly bi-generated Ranis (Archie Panjabi) traveling back to 1865 Bavaria to steal away a baby who was born as the seventh son of a seventh son and a seventh son, making him part of the pantheon of gods and giving him the ability to grant wishes. She brings the baby forward to 2025 where Conrad (Jonah Hauer-King), who we met in the previous episode [“Lucky Day”](https://outfrontmagazine.com/tv-review-doctor-who-episode-lucky-day-is-an-emotional-gut-punch/), uses it to wish into being a new world.

The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) wakes up as a man named John Smith, living in domestic bliss with his companion Belinda (Varada Sethu) as a married couple with a baby named Poppy (Sienna-Robyn Mavanga-Phipps) who was previously seen in the episode [“Space Babies.”](https://outfrontmagazine.com/tv-review-doctor-who-presents-a-double-season-premiere-of-varying-quality/) John Smith works at an insurance company while his wife stays home with the baby, but every now and then they have doubts about the world they’re living in, which cause the fabric of reality to tear and causes things like coffee mugs to fall through tables. If people express enough doubts, then they are reported to the police who take them away.

But there are people who can have more doubts than most. Former U.N.I.T. scientific advisor Shirley (Ruth Madeley), who is disabled, has been reduced to begging for spare change like most disabled people in Wish World. But disabled people can see that something is wrong with the world because Wish World doesn’t really have a place for them in society, so they sit on the edges and can see everything that’s wrong with it. Somehow, the Doctor’s former companion Ruby (Millie Gibson) can also see the flaws in reality as well as the disabled people and teams up with them to begin the takedown of Wish World.

![Image 11: Doctor Who](https://outfrontmagazineimages.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/26124655/dws2_220424_sd_146_2d2f5933.jpeg)

_Photo courtesy of Samuel Dore/BBC Studios/Disney/Bad Wolf_

One night, the Doctor receives a message on his television from Rogue (Jonathan Groff), The Doctor’s love interest from the episode [“Rogue,”](https://outfrontmagazine.com/tv-review-doctor-who-episode-rogue-gives-the-doctor-his-first-queer-male-romance/) telling him that “tables don’t do that,” leading the Doctor to start seeing there’s something seriously wrong with the world. He and Belinda are taken away to the Ranis’ (Panjabi and Anita Dobson) headquarters where it’s revealed that the Doctor’s doubt was the whole reason for the creation of the Wish World. The more the Doctor doubts, the more the fabric of reality tears, giving the Ranis the chance to bring back a classic series villain who has been lost for a very long time called Omega. The Ranis toss the Doctor from a tall height to die, but as the Doctor plunges to his death, he reveals that Poppy is a real baby, and that’s going to be important to what is to come next.

When the Rani started talking about bringing back “The One Who Was Lost,” I felt like it was likely going to be Omega. Bringing back The Master would be too easy and obvious after a surprise reveal like the Rani, and I knew it had to be someone a little more obscure. I narrowed it down to the Meddling Monk, the Valeyard, or Omega. The Meddling Monk was, potentially, too obscure and lacked the grandeur of Omega. The Valeyard’s storyline in the 1980s was so convoluted that the head writer back then sent out a memo telling writers not to address him. So that left Omega as the obvious choice. I almost wished they had gone for the Valeyard because it would have been more surprising and ambitious.

![Image 12](https://outfrontmagazineimages.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/26124934/jpp-who-170524-04547_7cba146d.jpeg)Omega is one of the founders of Time Lord society who helped create the Time Lords’ ability to travel through time. However, his experiment that created time travel sent him into an antimatter dimension where he lived for centuries, harboring resentment towards the Time Lords for abandoning him to his fate. His first appearance came in the show’s 10th anniversary special in 1973 when the Time Lords brought together the first three Doctors (William Hartnell, Patrick Troughton, and John Pertwee) to battle Omega (Stephen Thorne). But it turned out that Omega’s time in the antimatter dimension had left him with no physical form and he was only consciousness.

The three Doctors banish Omega back to his antimatter universe, as does the 5th Doctor (Peter Davison) when Omega (Ian Collier) tries to make a comeback in the 1983 episode “Arc of Infinity.” How they did so is overly complicated, as the classic series frequently was, but what you need to know is that he’s still stuck in the antimatter universe with no body, just pure consciousness. So if the Ranis are bringing Omega back from his imprisonment, he’ll definitely need a body, and my guess is they’re going to try to give him Conrad’s.

![Image 13: Doctor Who](https://outfrontmagazineimages.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/26125032/090524-jpp-who-09979_275aef47.jpeg)The episode does a great job of making us really hate Conrad and the Ranis and the whole world they created. The socio-political commentary that runs through this episode is likely to further infuriate those who complain that the show is getting too woke, but that’s exactly the point. _Doctor Who_ isn’t for those people anyway and it never has been. The episode sets up a situation where we really can’t wait to see Conrad and the Ranis get their comeupance as they created the perfect heteronormative hellscape, and next week’s episode promises to be a satisfying conclusion to this intricate web that Russell T. Davies has created. While I wish that he had brought back someone a little less obvious than Omega, the rest of the episode is such a perfect commentary that I can forgive the slightly obvious twist at the end of the episode.

Rating: 91/100
